indicators.note: in a down clue the word reads the same going up the grid as coming down it

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: An instruction to paddle a boat back and forth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up and down' tells you the answer reads the same in both directions, so it is a palindrome; the definition does the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A kayak is a small canoe-like boat propelled with a double-bladed paddle.

clue.text: I ring the boss before arriving at the work-room

indicators.note: the boss piece is placed in front of the other letters

parts.note: a stud is a raised knob or boss on a surface
a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone gives their boss a phone call just before reaching the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I ring the boss' reads as a phone call; in fact 'boss' means a stud (a raised knob), and 'before' puts STUD ahead of I and O.
explanation.definitionFit: A studio is an artist's or broadcaster's workplace, a room where work is done.

clue.text: It's clear the girl has a cute wiggle

parts.note: Eva is a girl's name

indicators.note: to wiggle is to move about, so the letters of a cute are jiggled into a new order

explanation.surface: Plainly the young woman sways her hips in a cute way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wiggle' looks like a dance move by the girl, but it shuffles the letters of 'a cute'. 'It's' is only a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To evacuate a building is to clear it of people.

parts.note: a living is a clergyman's benefice, so the pay that comes with a church living is a cleric's regular salary

explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'A living wage?' with its spaces lost. It looks like the campaign for fair pay, but 'living' is the church sense: the income of a vicar's benefice.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is a fixed salary, especially one paid to a member of the clergy.

clue.text: Man, for example, follows man in English city

indicators.note: the island piece comes after the name piece

parts.note: Carl is a man's name
the Isle of Man is an island in the Irish Sea, so Man is an example of an isle

explanation.surface: A sentence about one man coming after another in some English city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' with a capital is the Isle of Man, not a person; the capital is hidden by sentence position.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlisle is a cathedral city in Cumbria, in the far north-west of England.

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of stayed and for might form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Maybe someone stayed on through to Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday is traditionally the sabbath, the weekly day set aside from work.

clue.text: Entrance the prisoner is put out at

indicators.note: the prisoner word is placed outside, wrapping round the two letters of at

parts.note: a captive is a prisoner

explanation.surface: The jailbird is turned out of somewhere, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' looks like a noun (a doorway) but is the verb, to enchant; 'is put out' means the prisoner word goes outside 'at'.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to enchant and hold their attention completely.

clue.text: One with no faith in father bac king a horse

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: the printed 'bac king' is backing, so the horse word is turned round

parts.note: a nag is an old or poor horse

explanation.surface: An unbeliever's dad puts money on a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The page splits 'backing' into 'bac king'. It reads as betting on the horse, but it signals reversal of the horse word, which then follows father.
explanation.definitionFit: A pagan follows no mainstream religion, a heathen without the established faith.

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: offal is waste or refuse, especially butchers' scraps

explanation.surface: Nearly turn down the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refuse' looks like a verb (decline) but is the noun, rubbish. Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia, an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in central England.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa was the Anglo-Saxon ruler of Mercia, famous for building Offa's Dyke.

clue.text: In which all entrants won't come up to scratch

definitions.text: In which all entrants won't come up to scratch

parts.words: In which all entrants won't come up to scratch
parts.note: in this kind of race runners start from different marks, so most do not begin from the scratch line; read as an insult it says the field is poor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not up to scratch' sounds like poor quality, but in racing 'scratch' is the starting line for the unaided competitor; others are given starts or weights.
explanation.definitionFit: A handicap is a race in which competitors are given different starts or weights to even the contest.

clue.text: Chap went down with a cry of pain

parts.note: fell is the past tense of fall, to go down
ow is what someone says when hurt

explanation.surface: A man tumbled over and yelped.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellow and chap are both informal words for a man.

parts.note: so (soh) is a note of the sol-fa scale
fa is another note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A concert programme saying chairs are available.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, 'Notes', supplies two sol-fa notes side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A sofa is a long upholstered seat for several people, a piece of seating.

parts.note: the biblical vessel took animals aboard two by two, so no creature came on alone

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a boarding house with no single rooms; the boarders are animals, admitted only in pairs.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, the patriarch's vessel carried animals in pairs to survive the Flood.

clue.text: Soldiers in camp sorry, on manoeuvres

indicators.note: troops on manoeuvres move about, so the letters of camp and sorry are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: A soldier apologises while out on military exercises at camp.
explanation.definitionFit: An army corps is a large military formation made up of several divisions of troops.

indicators.note: outfit read as a verb, to fit out, signals the letters of a dreary are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wearing dull clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outfit' looks like the noun for clothes but works as the anagram signal: A stays as it is, then DREARY is rearranged into RRAYED.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrayed means clothed or decked out, especially in fine garments.

definitions.meaning: a union of parties joined for a common purpose
a marriage or union of two parties

explanation.definitionFit: An alliance is both a league of allies and a union such as a marriage, which is also called a match.

clue.text: It makes sense if it is used to win at cards

definitions.text: it is used to win at cards

indicators.note: the letters of the answer are rearranged to make the words sense if, read here as an anagram signal

explanation.surface: A remark that clever play at bridge is only common sense.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'It makes sense if' as: the answer rearranged makes SENSE IF. A finesse is a bridge move to take a trick with a lower card.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge or whist, a finesse is a trick-winning play using a lower card while a higher one is held out.

indicators.note: unusual suggests the letters of tidiness appear in an unusual arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone kept things remarkably neat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maintained' suggests upkeep and neatness; here it means asserted.
explanation.definitionFit: To insist is to maintain or assert something firmly.

definitions.meaning: those entered in a race or contest
items written into a register or log

explanation.definitionFit: Entries are both people entered in a competition and items written into a ledger or diary.

indicators.note: putting things in order rearranges them, so the letters of cancel and my are sorted afresh

explanation.surface: A customer withdraws a garden-centre purchase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' looks like a purchase to be cancelled but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyclamen is a flowering plant of the primrose family with upswept petals.

indicators.note: the power word is spoken, and what is heard is spelt differently

parts.note: might means strength or power

explanation.surface: Children wielding influence by being loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A mite is a small child, as in 'poor little mite'.

definitions.meaning: an old name for a dry white wine from Spain or the Canaries

explanation.definitionFit: To sack is to dismiss an employee; sack was also the old name for sherry-type wine, as drunk by Falstaff.

parts.note: it reads as preparing for the season, but means bending low before a leap

explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' looks like the season; it is a jump, which a cat makes after bending low.
explanation.definitionFit: To crouch is to bend low with knees bent, as an animal does before leaping.

clue.text: Hollywood success means no thing to Mark

parts.note: nothing is zero, written as the letter O
a scar is a mark left on the skin

explanation.surface: A film award counts for nothing to someone called Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name; it is a blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette is Hollywood's emblem of a winning film or performance.

clue.text: Could be Mr A to Z of music

definitions.text: Could be Mr A to Z of music

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters of Mr A to Z can be rearranged into another name

explanation.surface: A composer so complete he might be called the A to Z of music.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: the composer can be thought of as the complete A to Z of music.
explanation.definitionFit: The composer of The Magic Flute is one of the most complete masters of classical music.

clue.text: Possibly press one for an answer

indicators.note: possibly signals that press and one might be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: An automated phone menu: press 1 to reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a phone menu; 'Possibly' rearranges PRESS ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A response is a reply or answer.

indicators.note: wildly signals the letters of paces are scattered into another order

explanation.surface: Someone frantically walks up and down the room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'room' reads as a chamber, but means space, as in elbow room.
explanation.definitionFit: Room in the sense of free area or capacity to move.

clue.text: She cleans out for the steward

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of she cleans are put out of their order

explanation.surface: A woman does the cleaning for the head of the household.
explanation.definitionFit: A seneschal was the steward in charge of a medieval noble's household.
